nameStory: Creeping Jenny gets its name from its wandering habit - it creeps along the ground, sending out runners that spread in all directions like a person named Jenny might roam through a garden. It's also called moneywort because its round, coin-shaped leaves reminded people of old pennies, earning it other money-themed names like 'herb twopence' and 'twopenny grass.'
description: Creeping Jenny is a low-growing perennial that forms dense mats of trailing stems along the ground. Its bright green, perfectly round leaves grow in opposite pairs along stems that can stretch several feet in length. In summer, cheerful yellow cup-shaped flowers appear singly where the leaves meet the stem. This member of the primrose family stays low to the ground, rarely rising more than a few inches tall, but spreads widely to create a living carpet.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Perfectly round to oval leaves about the size of quarters, arranged in opposite pairs along the stem. They feel smooth and slightly fleshy, with a bright green color that may have a slight waxy feel.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers with 5 petals that form shallow cups, appearing singly where leaves attach to the stem. Each flower is about an inch across and has a cheerful, buttercup-like appearance.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms extensive mats by sending out long, trailing stems that root at the nodes (joints) where they touch the ground. Stems feel somewhat succulent and snap cleanly when broken.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, round stems that trail along the ground rather than standing upright. They have a slightly fleshy texture and root easily wherever they touch moist soil.

habitat: Creeping Jenny thrives in moist to wet soils and can be found along stream banks, pond edges, ditches, and wet meadows throughout New England. It also commonly escapes cultivation and can be found in moist garden areas, lawn edges, and anywhere water collects. This adaptable plant tolerates both sun and partial shade but prefers consistently moist conditions.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges early, with fresh bright green leaves appearing on spreading stems as the weather warms.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period with bright yellow flowers appearing from June through August. This is when the plant is most noticeable and easiest to identify.
seasonality.fall: Flowering winds down and leaves may begin to yellow slightly, though the plant often stays green well into autumn in mild weather.
seasonality.winter: In protected areas, some leaves may persist through winter, though most of the above-ground growth dies back, leaving the root system ready to regrow in spring.

funFact: Creeping Jenny can actually survive completely underwater for months at a time, making it popular in water gardens and aquariums - it's one of the few plants that can live both as a terrestrial ground cover and as a fully aquatic plant!
confusionNotes: The round, opposite leaves make creeping Jenny quite distinctive, but it might be confused with other trailing plants like ground ivy (which has scalloped, heart-shaped leaves) or partridgeberry (which has evergreen leaves with white veining). Remember: if the leaves are perfectly round like coins and arranged in neat opposite pairs, it's likely creeping Jenny.
contextualKnowledge: Though beautiful and useful as ground cover, creeping Jenny is actually native to Europe and can be quite aggressive in spreading, sometimes crowding out native plants in wet areas. Many gardeners love it for covering difficult wet spots, but it's worth keeping an eye on its spread in natural areas.
compareHints: Among its loosestrife relatives in New England, creeping Jenny is unique for its trailing, mat-forming habit - most other Lysimachia species stand upright. While whorled loosestrife has leaves arranged in circles around the stem and swamp candles grows tall with spikes of flowers, creeping Jenny stays low with its distinctive opposite, round leaves and single flowers at leaf joints.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its loosestrife relatives that tend to be taller with yellow flowers and different leaf arrangements, northern starflower is much shorter with its distinctive white seven-petaled blooms and single whorl of leaves.
Among New England's many Lysimachia species, whorled loosestrife is instantly recognizable by its four-leaf whorls - no other loosestrife has this arrangement.
Among its loosestrife relatives, swamp candles is unique for its tall, narrow flower spike - most other Lysimachia species have flowers in leaf axils or shorter, broader clusters.
Among New England's loosestrifes, fringed loosestrife is distinctive for its opposite leaves with fringed leaf stems and nodding yellow flowers.
Dotted loosestrife stands out from its loosestrife cousins mainly by those telltale petal spots - no other Lysimachia species has them.
Unlike its loosestrife cousins in the same genus, scarlet pimpernel stays ground-hugging rather than growing upright, and its flowers are much smaller but more intensely colored.
Among the loosestrife family in New England, gooseneck loosestrife is the only one with the distinctive curved white flower spikes.
Unlike its loosestrife relatives that are mostly freshwater plants with showy yellow or white flowers, sea milkwort is the oddball of the family - adapted for salt water and lacking petals entirely.

Yellow loosestrife stands out from its loosestrife relatives by its tall stature and dense yellow flower clusters - most other Lysimachia species in New England are shorter with more scattered flowers.
Among its loosestrife cousins, tufted loosestrife is unique for having flowers that emerge from the sides of the stem rather than at the tips.

Among New England's yellow-flowered loosestrifes, lowland loosestrife is distinguished by its flowers tucked into leaf axils rather than arranged in showy spikes like swamp candles, or whorled around the stem like whorled loosestrife.
Among its loosestrife relatives, lanceleaf loosestrife is distinguished by its alternate (not opposite or whorled) leaf arrangement and narrow, lance-shaped leaves.
Unlike its flashy cousin creeping Jenny (regular moneywort), miniature moneywort is truly miniature in every way - much smaller leaves, tinier flowers, and more delicate growth.

Unlike other Lysimachia species in New England that tend to be taller perennials with yellow flowers (like whorled loosestrife or swamp candles), blue scarlet pimpernel is a tiny blue-flowered annual that creeps along the ground.
